summary:
Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated US territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Screening at Guam's airport follows federal Transport Security Administration procedure. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers; travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports, a rule that applies to arrivals here.

Guam recognises same-sex marriage. Chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down the territory's prohibition on 5 June 2015, following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero after they were denied a licence; the ruling took effect at 8am on 9 June 2015 and made Guam the first US territory to recognise such marriages.
tangentialFactors:
A January 2025 executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly in the United States military and directed Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to submit an implementation plan within 30 days, framing trans identity as 'radical gender ideology'. Guam hosts a large permanent United States military presence, so the exclusion reaches a substantial share of the island's residents and workplaces rather than a marginal group.

The federal measures on markers, screening and military service bear directly on an island whose economy and society are shaped by that permanent basing, which also concentrates federal employers and federally funded providers in a small jurisdiction.

Guam's 2015 marriage ruling shows the territory courts have at times moved ahead of, or independently of, the federal political branches on recognition, even as the document, screening and funding rules imposed from Washington now govern entry and care here.
localsOnly:
The federal document rules that bind visitors also bind residents: changing a gender marker on a United States passport is governed by the January 2025 executive order, which reflects sex assigned at birth and eliminated the X marker.

The January 2025 order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care affects the federally funded providers that Guam residents rely on, not only care sought by visitors.

Trans service members and applicants within Guam's substantial military community are barred from serving openly under the January 2025 order.

Residents have been able to marry a same-sex partner since 9 June 2015, under the ruling of the United States District Court for the District of Guam.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two listed sources, a University of Hawaiʻi Pacific sexual identity guide and a Transgender Law Center Guam documents page, yield no usable finding for this record, so no claim rests on them.

Whether Guam's own territory-level statutes prohibit discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations is unresolved in this inventory; no Guam statute or local case is cited here.

The scope of the February 2025 visa-denial announcement is stated for athletes entering to compete in women's sports; its bearing on other visitor categories is unresolved and not sourced.

Local Guam police practice, hate-crime charging, and any territory-level complaint mechanism for trans residents are not addressed by the sources and remain unverified.
